item.title: Windows on Arm can run native Arm and emulated x64 code in the same app, something Apple never let Macs do
item.itunes:title: Windows on Arm can run native Arm and emulated x64 code in the same app, something Apple never let Macs do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Apple made the transition to Apple Silicon, apps could either be compiled and run natively for Arm, or they could be compiled and run as x86_64 applications through Rosetta. However, it's a distinct choice; pick one or the other, you can't do both. Windows on Arm does a similar thing to emulate x64 apps too, except Microsoft went a step further: a single Windows process can run native Arm code alongside emulated x64 code. That's thanks to Arm64EC.

Arm64EC is an application binary interface (ABI) announced by Microsoft in 2021 alongside Windows 11 on Arm. Arm64EC makes it possible to do things like run old x64 add-ins with Office on Arm, and Windows itself can change how much of itself runs natively when an x64 app calls into it. On the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 that I've been testing, Nvidia's driver package for the RTX Spark packs most of its user-mode components twice: once as plain Arm64 and once as Arm64EC.

It's got a bit of a trade-off, though. Arm64EC code has fewer CPU registers available while indirect calls also have to pass through an extra check to determine whether they're calling Arm or x64 code. What's more, it's not an Arm-defined standard, as it's a Microsoft-specific design, but Wine has implemented support for it, too.

Arm64EC is Arm code that follows x64's rules

EC stands for Emulation Compatible

An ABI defines the set of rules that compiled code, allowing separately built pieces to work together. This can be things like which registers carry a function's arguments, how structures are laid out in memory, where the return value goes, that kind of thing. x64 Windows has one set of rules and normal Arm64 Windows has another, which is why an Arm64 program can't load an x64 DLL. Arm64EC, though, introduces a third set, where Its instructions are real Arm64 instructions running natively on the CPU, but it follows x64-compatible software conventions for things like data structures and stack layout. It still retains much of Arm64's calling conventions.

What this means is that, in practice, code that gets compiled as Arm64EC identifies itself as x64 to any existing architecture checks. If you compile an application for Arm64EC, the compiler will define an _M_AMD64 macro used by x64 builds, and any application asking if it's built for x64 will be told that it is. Data structures also follow x64's layout rules, and compiled Arm64EC executables contain an x64 machine type in their header. The system knows, though, and Task Manager will show these apps as "ARM64 (x64 compatible)." This only applies to x64, though, as 32-bit x86 apps still use the older WOW64 emulation layer.

The biggest reason for all of this, though, is plugin support. Before Microsoft introduced Arm64EC, porting an app to Arm was "all-or-nothing," in Microsoft's words. If your app loads third-party DLLs into its own process that you don't control, such as an Office add-in or an audio plugin for a DAW, you would need to wait for the original developer to also port their code. Arm64EC makes this a lot easier, as you can recompile your own code as native Arm while loading x64 plugins under Prism emulation in the same process.

This is how Microsoft built its 64-bit Office for Arm, allowing "existing x64 plugins will work seamlessly." The company says that most of the operating system code loaded by an x64 app on Arm is compiled as Arm64EC, which means much of the Windows code an emulated app calls into runs natively. The concept has roots in Microsoft's older Compiled Hybrid PE, or CHPE, first demonstrated at Build 2017, which similarly combined Arm64 code with x86 compatibility.

Arm64EC gives up some registers to stay compatible with x64

They're incompatible, and there's nowhere to save them

Arm64 has 31 general-purpose registers and 32 vector registers, whereas x64 has 16-general-purpose registers and, without AVX-512, 16 vector registers. That's especially a problem for Windows, as it represents a thread's CPU state using a structure called CONTEXT, which exception handling, debuggers, and APIs like GetThreadContext rely on. Because Windows has been built on x86_64 assumptions, x64 code expects that structure to have an x64 layout.

Arm64EC gets around this by retaining the x64 structure, making it so the Arm registers that are used all fit into the x64 CONTEXT structure. X0 maps to RCX, X1 maps to RDX, the stack pointer maps to RSP, the program counter maps to RIP, and so on. Some of the mappings are a bit odd, as a handful of Arm registers (X6, X7, X9 through X12, X15, and the link register) get stashed in the slots for x87 floating-point registers.

Whatever doesn't fit is disallowed entirely, which includes X13, X14, X23, X24, or X28, and it can't touch vector registers V16 through V31. Long-time Microsoft engineer Raymond Chen explained that their values "are not preserved across context switches or asynchronous exceptions. (There's nowhere to save them!)" Microsoft chose the mapping in a way that still keeps all the registers used by normal Arm64 calling conventions available, making it so that Arm64EC functions can call eachother much like they do in native Arm64 code.

There are some exceptions, namely variadic functions like printf. These use x64-like argument-passing rules, with only the first four argument positions eligible for registers. This restriction means that the compiler has fewer registers to keep values in, which can introduce overhead.

Thunks and call checkers handle every jump between the two

A layer has to act as a translator

Even when both systems have matching data layouts, Arm64 and x64 disagree on where a function's arguments belong. Microsoft's own example is a function that takes an int, a double, another int, and another double. On Arm64, those will go in X0, D0, X1, and D1, while on x64 they go in in RCX, XMM1, R8, and XMM3. A small piece of glue code, called a "thunk", handles the conversion depending on the type and position of each argument.

An entry thunk handles x64 code that calls into Arm64EC, rearranging the arguments from x64's layout into Arm's. There's also an exit thunk which does the same thing in reverse when Arm64EC code calls into something that could be x64. The problem is that the compiler itself often can't know what architecture it's calling, as a function pointer could point at native Arm code or emulated x64 code, which might only become clear at runtime. Microsoft dealt with this by having indirect calls in Arm64EC go through a "call checker" that's provided by Windows. If the target is Arm64EC, the call proceeds natively. If it's x64, the checker routes it through the exit thunk and into the emulator.

In order to make that work, Arm64EC binaries have a table built in that says which of their code pages contain Arm64EC instructions and which contain x64 instructions. Functions in Arm64EC also reserve four bytes immediately before their first instruction to store a relative offset to their entry thunk, so that when the emulator encounters x64 code calling an Arm64EC function, it uses that offset to find the correct thunk. Finally, code generated at runtime by a JIT compiler is treated as x64 by default, so .NET, Java, and other unmodified x64 runtimes keep working.

For Windows applications that hook system functions by overwriting their first few instructions, those programs expect to find x64 instructions. By default, Arm64EC DLLs will provide a tiny x64 stub for each exported functions, which Microsoft calls a "fast-forward sequence." This redirects execution to the real Arm64EC code, and if nothing modified it, Windows skips the the stub entirely. If something has hooked it, the emulator will execute the modified version in order to keep the hook intact.

This is why there's overhead associated with Arm64EC; every indirect Arm64EC call requires a check, even when both sides are native, and calls crossing into x64 code need a thunk and a transition into the emulator. Direct calls between Arm64EC functions, though, are just normal Arm calls.

Arm64X is another piece of Microsoft's solution here, as it's a file format capable of packing both normal Arm64 code and Arm64EC code into a single file. Microsoft's analogy compares it to old red-and-blue 3D images, where "an x64 app sees the DLL as though it's an x64 DLL, while an Arm64 app sees the same DLL as an Arm64 DLL." Arm64X is used by Windows for the system DLLs that both x64 and Arm64 apps need from System32, which allows the company to use a single folder of x64 system files unlike the SysWOW64 folder used for 32-bit x86 apps. It's also useful for developers who need to support both, as normal Arm64 and Arm64EC processes can't directly load each other's DLLs.

macOS never lets Intel and Arm code share a process

They can work together, just not in the same place

Apple's approach to Rosetta and Apple silicon is entirely different, with the company's official documentation stating that "The system prevents you from mixing arm64 code and x86_64 code in the same process. Rosetta translation applies to an entire process, including all code modules that the process loads dynamically." If a native Arm app tries to load an Intel-only plugin into the same process, the system will throw an error instead.

This doesn't mean that Intel and Arm code can't work together on a Mac; they just can't share a process. Apple's own suggestion is to run plugins in separate processes, allowing them to communicate over XPC. This means one service for arm64 plugins and another for x86_64 ones, and Audio Units are some of the best-known examples. macOS has a built-in AUHostingCompatibilityService that runs Intel-only AU plugins outside of the host, which programs like Ableton use to support Intel-based plugins. Intel-only VST2 and VST3 plugins still won't work this way, and the only solution Ableton is to run the entire DAW through Rosetta instead.

Apple never wanted to keep Intel code around forever, which it clearly signalled when it chose to make the C++ ABI on Apple silicon match "the ABI for iOS devices, and not the ABI for Intel-based Mac computers." Rosetta even has a shelf-life, as it will only continue to exist as a general-purpose tool "through macOS 27." Microsoft has no equivalent for x64 emulation on Windows, and Arm64EC is very much a product of a platform where old x64 code is expected to keep running.

Arm64EC is a Microsoft design, but Microsoft isn't the only one using it

Wine implemented it too

Arm64EC isn't a formally standardised ABI, with Microsoft saying that the normal Arm64 ABI on Windows "usually follows ARM's standard AArch64 EABI." Arm's own ABI specifications for AArch64 make no mention of Arm64EC, either. This is a Windows-specific design built around Microsoft's x64 emulation system, which Microsoft documents rather than Arm.

Arm64EC is also a lot of work for anyone else to support. In 2024, the maintainer of the llvm-mingw toolchain, Martin Storsjö, once said that "ARM64EC is a totally different thing though; that's an entirely separate ABI on almost every single level" in the GCC mailing list. GCC was only getting support for normal Windows on Arm at the time, and it seems that to this day, Arm64EC isn't supported in GCC. LLVM has supported it since version 18.1, and Rust offers it as a Tier 2 target, though the maintainer listed for Rust's Arm64EC target is a Microsoft developer.

Wine has one of the few independent implementaions, and support arrived with Wine 10.0 in January 2025. It was one of the main highlights of the release, and the same release also added an x86-64 emulation interface that "takes advantage of the ARM64EC support to run all of the Wine code as native, with only the application's x86-64 code requiring emulation." Wine doesn't have its own x86-64 emulator, but FEX, an x86 emulator for Arm Linux, implements that interface when built as Arm64EC. This is why there's overhead associated with Arm64EC; every indirect Arm64EC call requires a check, even when both sides are native, and calls crossing into x64 code need a thunk and a transition into the emulator. Direct calls between Arm64EC functions, though, are just normal Arm calls.

Arm64X is another piece of Microsoft's solution here, as it's a file format capable of packing both normal Arm64 code and Arm64EC code into a single file. Microsoft's analogy compares it to old red-and-blue 3D images, where "an x64 app sees the DLL as though it's an x64 DLL, while an Arm64 app sees the same DLL as an Arm64 DLL." Arm64X is used by Windows for the system DLLs that both x64 and Arm64 apps need from System32, which allows the company to use a single folder of x64 system files unlike the SysWOW64 folder used for 32-bit x86 apps. It's also useful for developers who need to support both, as normal Arm64 and Arm64EC processes can't directly load each other's DLLs.

macOS never lets Intel and Arm code share a process

They can work together, just not in the same place

Apple's approach to Rosetta and Apple silicon is entirely different, with the company's official documentation stating that "The system prevents you from mixing arm64 code and x86_64 code in the same process. Rosetta translation applies to an entire process, including all code modules that the process loads dynamically." If a native Arm app tries to load an Intel-only plugin into the same process, the system will throw an error instead.

This doesn't mean that Intel and Arm code can't work together on a Mac; they just can't share a process. Apple's own suggestion is to run plugins in separate processes, allowing them to communicate over XPC. This means one service for arm64 plugins and another for x86_64 ones, and Audio Units are some of the best-known examples. macOS has a built-in AUHostingCompatibilityService that runs Intel-only AU plugins outside of the host, which programs like Ableton use to support Intel-based plugins. Intel-only VST2 and VST3 plugins still won't work this way, and the only solution Ableton is to run the entire DAW through Rosetta instead.

Apple never wanted to keep Intel code around forever, which it clearly signalled when it chose to make the C++ ABI on Apple silicon match "the ABI for iOS devices, and not the ABI for Intel-based Mac computers." Rosetta even has a shelf-life, as it will only continue to exist as a general-purpose tool "through macOS 27." Microsoft has no equivalent for x64 emulation on Windows, and Arm64EC is very much a product of a platform where old x64 code is expected to keep running.

Arm64EC is a Microsoft design, but Microsoft isn't the only one using it

Wine implemented it too

Arm64EC isn't a formally standardised ABI, with Microsoft saying that the normal Arm64 ABI on Windows "usually follows ARM's standard AArch64 EABI." Arm's own ABI specifications for AArch64 make no mention of Arm64EC, either. This is a Windows-specific design built around Microsoft's x64 emulation system, which Microsoft documents rather than Arm.

Arm64EC is also a lot of work for anyone else to support. In 2024, the maintainer of the llvm-mingw toolchain, Martin Storsjö, once said that "ARM64EC is a totally different thing though; that's an entirely separate ABI on almost every single level" in the GCC mailing list. GCC was only getting support for normal Windows on Arm at the time, and it seems that to this day, Arm64EC isn't supported in GCC. LLVM has supported it since version 18.1, and Rust offers it as a Tier 2 target, though the maintainer listed for Rust's Arm64EC target is a Microsoft developer.

Wine has one of the few independent implementaions, and support arrived with Wine 10.0 in January 2025. It was one of the main highlights of the release, and the same release also added an x86-64 emulation interface that "takes advantage of the ARM64EC support to run all of the Wine code as native, with only the application's x86-64 code requiring emulation." Wine doesn't have its own x86-64 emulator, but FEX, an x86 emulator for Arm Linux, implements that interface when built as Arm64EC. Arm apps can be run on Linux with the same techniques used by Windows, with one caveat: Wine 10.0 requires a 4K memory page size, "since that is what the Windows ABI specifies."

At the end of the day, Apple has a significantly simpler approach, but that's helped by the fact that it owns the entire macOS ecosystem. Windows has decades of assumptions of compatibility built in, and Arm64EC is what you get when that old software still needs to work. It may not be perfect, but Microsoft's approach to Arm is leaps and bounds ahead of what it was just a few years ago.

item.title: I put a local AI model on a bootable USB, so I can troubleshoot a dead PC with a chatbot that doesn't need the internet
item.itunes:title: I put a local AI model on a bootable USB, so I can troubleshoot a dead PC with a chatbot that doesn't need the internet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Bootable Linux USB drives are useful for getting into a PC when Windows refuses to start. You can inspect the internal drive, copy your files, and use recovery tools without loading the broken installation. I wanted to add something else to that setup – a chatbot that could help me understand what those tools were telling me, even without an internet connection.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I put a small local AI model on the same USB as a Linux rescue environment, complete with a browser interface for chatting. The computer supplies the processing power, and the software and model live on the drive. Once I boot into Linux, I can give the chatbot diagnostic output and ask questions as I work through the problem.

I put the entire setup on a USB

Linux, recovery tools, and a chatbot

I start with a 64GB USB 3 drive and install Ventoy on it. Ventoy lets me copy bootable ISO files onto the drive and choose which one to launch when the computer starts. The remaining space works as normal storage, where I keep the AI runtime and model files. Installing Ventoy erases the USB, so copy anything you need off it first.

For Linux, I use SystemRescue. It already includes disk diagnostics, partitioning tools, file recovery utilities, and Firefox. Those are useful when you’re investigating a broken Windows installation, and having them included saves me from downloading tools during the rescue session. SystemRescue doesn’t support Secure Boot out of the box, so check your firmware settings and have your BitLocker recovery key available before changing them.

The AI side uses llama.cpp with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. I choose the Q4_K_M version, which takes up about 2.5GB, and set the context to 2,048 tokens to keep memory use manageable on my 8GB Lenovo. I also use CPU inference, so the chatbot doesn’t depend on getting GPU drivers working inside the live environment.

I keep the Linux x86-64 runtime, its required libraries, and the GGUF model together on the USB. After booting SystemRescue, I mount the USB’s data partition and launch llama-server with the model’s local path. It includes a chat interface that I can open in Firefox.

My Linux desktop fits on a USB drive, and it boots the same on any PC I use

My full setup, wherever I go

12
By  João Carrasqueira

I give the chatbot actual diagnostic output

Understanding what the diagnostic tools report

Once the rescue desktop loads, establish what the computer can still detect and access. I usually start with lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS, which lists the connected drives and their partitions. Once you have the output, paste that into the chatbot alongside a description of the problem.

I also explain the environment before asking for advice. The installed operating system is Windows, but I’m currently running SystemRescue from a USB. My opening prompt looks something like this:

Windows won’t start, and I’m running SystemRescue from USB. Here is my lsblk output. Help me identify the internal Windows drive, explain what this output establishes, and suggest the next diagnostic check without modifying the disk.

From there, you can provide a drive-health report from smartctl or relevant storage messages from dmesg. These answer different questions. Seeing the SSD in the drive list establishes that Linux detects it. A health report provides information about the drive itself, and kernel messages can reveal errors encountered as Linux communicates with it.

This gives the conversation something concrete to work with. You can ask what a particular field means, why a suggested check matters, or whether the available evidence supports a diagnosis.

Back up files before repairing Windows

Getting important files onto another drive

Before making changes to the Windows installation, you’ll want to copy important files. SystemRescue already lets you access a Windows partition even when Windows itself won’t start, so you can use the same session to copy documents and other personal files to a separate external drive.

This is where you can make use of the drive information from the previous checks. You can ask the chatbot to help identify the source partition and explain where it is mounted. Windows user folders usually sit under Users on the system partition, but the path you use in Linux also includes that partition’s mount location. Giving the model the actual mount information helps it provide paths that match the machine in front of you.

You can connect another external drive for the backup. I keep the source partition mounted read-only and use the file manager to copy selected folders to the destination. If BitLocker protects the Windows volume, you’ll need to unlock it with the appropriate credentials before accessing its contents.

Local LLMs deserve more credit

I keep finding useful jobs for local LLMs, from organizing my browser history to helping me troubleshoot a PC. Plenty more are worth trying on hardware you already own. Don’t let anyone tell you local models are useless when you can put them to work on so much.

"Hey Claude, what's wrong with my PC?"

3

item.title: I tried every free emulator frontend, and the one I'd recommend isn't RetroArch
item.itunes:title: I tried every free emulator frontend, and the one I'd recommend isn't RetroArch
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Emulation used to be a complicated endeavor, even for some of the consoles we consider relatively simple today. But now, things have progressed so much that we often don't focus as much on the emulation part, but more on the interfaces that make it happen.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Frontends, as they're called, give you a user-friendly way to browse and play your games, and RetroArch is one of the most popular ones out there. But after trying every free frontend in active development, I don't think RetroArch is the best option out there.

There are more options than I thought

I still have a clear favorite, though

I'll start by admitting that I went into this project with a somewhat set idea in my mind. My favorite emulator frontend has long been ES-DE, and, aside from RetroArch and iiSU on Android, I hadn't really bothered looking into the possibility of others existing. But a quick search showed me there's a wide array of options out there, and a good few are still in active development today, and that was somewhat surprising.

What's perhaps less surprising is that other options aren't as popular for good reason. I tried Playnite, LaunchBox, GameEx, mGalaxy, Pegasus, and Simple Launcher, and almost all of these options have frustrating problems. Most have UIs that feel overly complicated or ugly, and others make setup harder than it should be.

I finally organized my emulator collection, and this free frontend made it feel better than a real console

It makes everything feel natural

2
By  João Carrasqueira

The only two I can recommend are Playnite and LaunchBox. Unlike ES-DE, they're not just frontends for emulation, and they can launch games from all kinds of platforms on PC, including Steam, Amazon, and others. They also have more mouse and keyboard-focused interfaces, compared to the more controller-focused UI of ES-DE.

Still, the polish of ES-DE is very hard to beat, and I actually prefer the HTPC focus of ES-DE, since I'd always rather play these games with a controller anyway.

ES-DE is customizable and beautiful

Plus it works perfectly with a controller

RetroArch and ES-DE both offer fairly user-friendly UIs, but in my opinion, it's extremely hard to top ES-DE. The default UI is already fantastic, but you can dive into dozens and dozens of themes that completely change the look and feel of the experience while retaining the ease of use of the base package.

ES-DE is also incredible in its presentation beyond the theme itself. Games are automatically organized by platform, and each platform itself is presented in a clean and beautiful way (depending on your theme, but the default is quite good already). But ES-DE also creates dedicated sections for your recent games and your favorites, so you can easily jump back into something you've played recently, which is great.

The built-in metadata scraper lets you download game icons, screenshots, descriptions, and even trailers, and it turns your game library into a lively collection that's just pleasant to peruse. Other frontends can also have metadata managers, but I found most of them much harder to get started with compared to ES-DE, which prompts you to download metadata when your first run it, and makes it easy to do subsequent runs as well.

Diving into all the settings available in ES-DE can be slightly intimidating at first, but it works and looks great out of the box, so you can dive into the extras at your own pace without it getting in the way of your experience. And the entire UI is very controller friendly, so you can browse every menu and find games quickly without ever needing a keyboard and mouse. If you ever wanted something that felt like a console for the living room, ES-DE lets you build the perfect solution.

Setup can be even easier

If you just dont have the time

Setting up ES-DE by itself is already relatively easy, but there are a few steps where you have to define directories for your ROMs, download emulators, and so on. It's not too hard to do, but what's so great about ES-DE is that, because it's clearly the best option, there are also some solutions out there that build upon it and make it even easier.

Of course, I'm talking about EmuDeck and, for Linux users, RetroDeck. EmuDeck is on all desktop platforms, but on Linux, I actually prefer RetroDeck, though you're perfectly well served either way.

What these tools do is they setup the entire emulation flow for you. They download ES-DE, emulators, and even create the folder structure for your ROMs. All you need to do then is move your ROm files into said structure to get started. These tools even present you with some ES-DE theme options during setup, so you don't have to go through the menus to find a more unique look for your setup.

Whether you use these tools or not, ES-DE is fantastic, but they do make it easier than ever to get started.

What about phones?

iiSU wins for Android

While PCs are still my go-to when it comes to emulation, there are many people who might prefer playing their games on their phones, and if that's you, you might be disappointed to find out that ES-DE for Android is actually a paid release. But if you want a great gaming frontend for Android, I'd have to recommend iiSU.

I first tried iiSU a few weeks back and even though it's still in its early stages, it's absolutely beautiful. It doesn't have all the theming options of ES-DE, but it still offers an easy setup process and a gorgeous UI with some configuration options to make it your own. Its look is inspired by platforms like the Wii U, Nintendo 3DS, and even Sony's XMB interface from the PlayStation 3 and PSP.

I wrote extensively about iiSU before, so I recommend checking out that article if you're curious to learn more.

RetroArch is still great

But for a different reason

While RetroArch isn't my choice of frontend for emulation, it still plays a major role in my emulation experience. I almost struggle to call RetroArch a frontend because to me, it's more like a middleman, and it does that job exceedingly well.

The thing is, while RetroArch can be a frontend, its best job is serving as a manager for different emulators, which operate as "cores" for RetroArch. Essentially, downloading an emulator no longer means opening your web browser, searching for the best emulators, and learning how each one works and how to configure them. RetroArch brings all these emulators under one roof, with a universal UI and an easy way to customize options for each one, while also making installs easy.

4 best operating systems you should consider for retro gaming emulation

There are many options to choose from

1
By  Anurag Singh

For most frontends, ES-DE included, RetroArch is seen as an emulator itself, and loading up a game using a specific core is simply using specific command arguments behind the scenes. It's all invisible, yet it all works perfectly. And if you use a solution like EmuDeck or RetroDeck, it will even download many emulator cores for you, so you barely have to do anything to set it up.

ES-DE is the best way to play your retro games

RetroArch is a popular frontend for emulation, but it can actually do a lot more, and work together with a solution like ES-DE for the best experience. Arguably, combining these two is the best way to get into retro gaming on your PC, while Android gamers can replace ES-DE with iiSU and still take advantage of that pairing. As a frontend, RetroArch isn't the best, but it still has its place.

item.itunes:title: I made Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity work together on one project instead of competing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent the better part of the last few months jumping from one AI coding tool to another. The big three are undoubtedly the ones I reach for most: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, and Google's Antigravity. One of my favorite things to do has been pitting them against each other to see which one comes out on top.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

However, after months of comparing them, I started wondering what would happen if I stopped treating them as competitors and got them to work together instead. After all, each has its own strengths, so why not put those strengths to use on the same project? So, that's exactly what I did. I made all three collaborate to build a study app from scratch, with each agent handling a different part of the project.

There are a few reason I use multiple AI coding agents

Why settle for one when you can use three?

If there's one thing I've learned from experimenting with different LLMs and coding agents, it's that each has its own strengths and weaknesses. While I now have my own preferences for which coding harness I reach for first and which ones I tend to avoid for certain tasks, I've realized that there's no single LLM that's the best at everything. After all, AI labs are constantly releasing newer models that improve upon their predecessors, and the model that excels at one task today might not necessarily be the best choice a few months down the line.

For instance, Codex was one of the tools that really grew on me over the last few months, and I was using it for practically all my coding-related tasks (and even a lot of non-coding tasks). However, after building just a tool or two, I realized its frontend capabilities were lacking. It'd build something technically solid, but the UI screamed vibe-coded from all angles, and I just couldn't get it to look the way I wanted without a lot of hand-holding.

I had gotten used to using Claude Design and Claude in general for frontend work, so I began to pair Codex with Claude Code. Gemini's models have almost always disappointed me when it comes to coding, but Argon 4 has been a massive update. I wrote about testing it against Opus 5.5 for MUO, and while I won't go as far as calling it the "best coder in the world" like Google did, Gemini surprised me massively with its frontend design and product decisions. So, Argon 4 has now made it to my list of coding agents I enjoy using alongside the others!

Beyond the fact that different models can make up for one another's weaknesses, there are plenty of other benefits to using multiple coding agents. For one, I'm no longer restricted by a single tool's usage limits. If I hit my limits with one agent, I can simply switch to another instead of putting my entire project on hold.

There's also the fact that I can have multiple agents working on different tasks simultaneously, rather than waiting for one to finish before moving on to the next. When you're working on larger projects with several moving parts, that can make a massive difference. Sure, you could technically use parallel agents within a single coding tool, but that still means relying on the same model or ecosystem for everything. By using different coding agents, I get to take advantage of what each one does best while getting multiple parts of a project done at the same time.

I used Orca to get all three agents working together

Orca was the glue that held everything together

Now, this is obviously not my first time using Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity in parallel. I've used the three to build a portfolio website, my dream note-taking app, complex mobile apps, landing pages, B2B websites, focus apps, and more. However, the process has always been a little messy. I'd have multiple terminal windows open, constantly jump between agents to check their progress, and manually keep track of what each one was working on.

This is when I went off to look for an app that would make managing multiple agents working in parallel easier. That's when I came across Orca, an open-source Agent Development Environment (ADE) that lets you run and manage multiple AI coding agents from one place. It supports Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenCode, Qwen Code, Hermes Agent and several other coding agents, bringing them all together under one roof.

While going through Orca's features, I came across its support for Git worktrees, which allow multiple coding agents to work on different parts of the same project simultaneously without interfering with one another's changes. That's what led to the idea behind this article. I decided to put all three agents to work simultaneously to build me a study app, with each one handling a different part of the project based on its strengths.

I assigned frontend development and UI design to Antigravity, backend development and database management to Claude Code, and the study algorithms and testing to Codex.

The coding process was quicker, more hands-off, and surprisingly impressive

Teamwork really does make the dream work

For this experiment, I decided to build a study app that would combine some of my favorite features from NotebookLM, Quizlet, and Anki. I'll talk about what I ended up building in a separate article very soon, but what I really want to talk about here is the process of building it, how well the three agents worked together, and whether getting them to collaborate actually made a difference compared to my usual approach.

I began by asking Claude Code to set up the foundation for the app, which I decided to call StudyLab. Rather than having it build the entire thing, I instructed it to create the project architecture, shared data models, API contracts, and an AGENTS.md file outlining which parts of the project each agent would be responsible for. Once that was done, I created three separate Git worktrees in Orca, all starting from the same foundation.

I assigned frontend development and UI design to Antigravity, backend development and database management to Claude Code, and the study algorithms, spaced repetition system, and testing to Codex. I then gave each agent a prompt explaining its responsibilities and let them get to work.

I changed one setting in Claude Code, and my token burn dropped by 45%

Claude Code was overthinking the assignment

8
By  Mahnoor Faisal

This is where things got interesting. Instead of having to wait for one agent to finish its work before moving on to another, all three were building different parts of StudyLab simultaneously. I could jump between their sessions in Orca, see what they were working on, and check their progress without having to manage multiple terminal windows. For the most part, I barely had to intervene.

Once all three agents finished, I returned to Claude Code and asked it to merge their contributions into a single application. I was expecting this to be the part where things would get messy, especially since the agents had been working independently. Surprisingly, though, there was only one merge conflict, and it involved a documentation file that both Claude and Codex had edited. Claude resolved it by preserving both changes, and the application passed its initial verification checks.

I also had Claude test the actual user experience. Its first attempt to do so through Chrome ran into a permissions issue, so I switched to Playwright for automated browser testing. Ultimately, all five user journeys passed, including creating courses, saving notes, reviewing flashcards, completing quizzes, and tracking progress. The project also passed 141 automated tests.

The best part is that I loved the result it produced. The interface felt polished, the different sections worked smoothly together, and everything I tried behaved the way I'd expect a proper study app to. My usage limits also didn't take the hit they usually do when I'm relying on a single coding agent to build an entire project. Since the workload was split across three different agents, I wasn't burning through one tool's limits as quickly as I normally would.

Three agents are officially better than one

Despite having three different agents working on three different parts of the application, the finished product felt surprisingly cohesive. There was very little back-and-forth required on my end, and I didn't have to spend hours manually fixing code to get the different components to communicate. For something that started as an experiment to see whether competing coding agents could collaborate, I couldn't have been happier with how it turned out.

Like thousands of other people, the first mesh VPN I tried was Tailscale, and it was because of word-of-mouth. For a while, it did most of what I needed, but when I wanted to take back control of each part of the chain, I attempted to trade it for a plain WireGuard setup with a VPS acting as the hub, but that had so many ease-of-use issues that I began hunting for another alternative, and I eventually found it in NetBird.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Just over 6 months ago, I finally made the switch to self-hosted NetBird, and it's still the thing I use to access everything in my home lab. The setup was painless, and it gave me the same kind of polish that Tailscale gave me, but on infrastructure that was my own.

Is Tailscale the safest way to access your home network remotely?

Tailscale is easy to set up, but is that trading off your security?

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The control plane runs on my server, not someone else's

I'm not reliant on a company to run the important layer

Every mesh VPN built on WireGuard has two halves: the data plane and the control plane. The data plane is the nuts and bolts of WireGuard, and it runs the encrypted tunnels between your devices. The control plane is the coordination layer that tells each device who its peers are, which keys to trust, and what it’s allowed to reach, and this is what NetBird's stack takes care of, and it includes three services. Its management server holds the peer configs and policies, the signal server negotiates connections between those peers and the relay carries the encrypted traffic when a direct path isn't possible.

With Tailscale or NetBird's conventional cloud deployment, a company is running that control plane layer for you. In my setup, all three services run on a minimum-spec VPS hosted in Toronto under my own domain. The stack isn't a community reimplementation of NetBird's cloud services, but a first-party version of the real thing, and it's completely open-source. Tailscale's clients are largely open-source too, but the control plane is closed-source, and while there is a self-hosted option in Headscale, it does not carry official support from Tailscale.

Day-to-day, compared to the cloud-based options, all of this is completely invisible to me, which is exactly how I want it. When I pull up Immich on my phone for a sync or stream Jellyfin from my media server, everything is being served from a machine I control, not through someone else's database.

Tailscale replaced my VPN, port forwarding, and dynamic DNS in one install

It's now an indispensable part of my home lab

3
By  Ayush Pande

There's no finite user count

I can add as many people as I'd like

The self-hosted Community Edition of NetBird doesn't require a license, doesn't have a time limit, no fees, and, perhaps most importantly to me, doesn't cap users or devices. I can add as many people and devices as I want to the mesh.

This wasn't a huge issue before, as both Tailscale and NetBird's cloud deployments have pretty generous limits on how many users and devices one can add, and most people won't hit that wall. It is nice, though, not to have the terms set by someone else. Tailscale has already reworked its plans more than once, and while the last change was actually good for free users, it's not a guarantee it stays that way.

There's also the cost of renting the VPS, which isn't free, but it does pull double-duty for me anyway. I need a publicly reachable server, as my ISP has put me behind CGNAT, so it acts as the solution to that as well as the hub for NetBird.

Tailscale's free plan replaced my $100-a-year VPN subscription

My tailnet does everything my old VPN did, minus the invoice.

2
By  Korbin Brown

It completely replaced my need to port forward

I didn't expect this, but it's super useful

The feature I didn't account for when I switched was the built-in reverse proxy, which I've used plenty since jumping over. It allows me to expose something like Jellyfin on my own domain without a single inbound port open at home, and it's still secure thanks to the ability to add layers of authentication on top of a username and password in the web client. NetBird also extended the proxy beyond HTTP with Layer 4 support for raw TCP, UDP and TLS passthrough, and that’s how my TeamSpeak server and game servers are reachable again. They used to be port forwards, but since my ISP put me behind CGNAT, that was no longer possible. Now, players connect to the proxy on my VPS, and their traffic reaches my home lab over the mesh with fairly minimal latency. For players that are within the same province as me, the latency is only about 10-15ms, which is well within the range of what it would be without the extra hop.

Tailscale's closest equivalent is Funnel, but its capabilities are more narrow. Funnel listens only on ports 443, 8443 and 10000, handles only TLS-encrypted connections, uses only your tailnet’s ts.net domain, and has bandwidth limits you can’t configure. This is perfectly reasonable for sharing a web app, but not for a voice server or game server that speaks UDP.

NetBird replaced Tailscale when I hit the 6-user limit, and it costs me $3 a month instead of $25

It used infrastructure I was already paying for

2
By  Ty Sherback

I'm taking on more risk by self-hosting

But I'm fine with the trade-off

If you're looking into remote access and all you need is to SSH onto a couple of machines and access your Jellyfin library through your phone, self-hosting the entire control plane doesn't have a ton of payoff. The cloud-based options from Tailscale and NetBird both get you there in minutes, and they handle all the updating and infrastructure concerns. And they're free. When you self-host this stuff, you're responsible if it goes down, and that includes keeping it secure.

I'm completely fine with taking on all of the above because of the control it affords me, and I haven't been able to find anything else that's open-source, self-hostable and free to use that has the same kind of feature set as NetBird. Headscale gets you there if you already have your entire setup on Tailscale and you wish to move it to a host that you control, but it doesn't have the same kind of support or features.

item.title: Intel's 8th-gen CPUs are the most underrated used chips you can buy
item.itunes:title: Intel's 8th-gen CPUs are the most underrated used chips you can buy
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Intel's 8th-gen CPUs launched almost a decade ago, so I wouldn't blame you for thinking they're practically obsolete at this point. After all, even today's entry-level Ryzen CPUs can put the "high-end" i7-8700K to shame in gaming benchmarks. But the point of those CPUs today isn't to prove they can still compete with what's available on the market. It's about how much performance you're getting for the money and whether you actually need anything faster for your use case.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

With RAM and GPU prices losing touch with reality this year, I think Intel's 8th-gen lineup deserves another look, especially if all you want is a general-purpose PC that can also handle some gaming when paired with an entry-level GPU like the RTX 3060. I was able to find i7-8700K listings on eBay for under $70 and even spotted Z370 motherboards for half that price. That's barely over $100 for a 6-core CPU and motherboard combo, which I think is a pretty good deal in 2026.

Nvidia's resurrection of the RTX 3060 proves that older GPUs still matter

One of the best budget cards of the last decade gets a new lease on life

3
By  Ty Sherback

It comes down to the two extra cores

We wouldn't be having this discussion if these were 4-core CPUs

Remember when Intel used to be obsessed with sticking to four cores for its mainstream CPUs year after year? Well, Coffee Lake ended that streak in 2017, shortly after AMD shook up the CPU market with its first-generation Ryzen processors. Intel's 8th-gen lineup brought 6 cores to both the Core i5 and i7 models, with hyperthreading being limited to the latter. That's a pretty significant jump considering even the flagship i7-7700K was stuck with four cores and eight threads despite launching the same year.

Fast forward to 2026, and even though we have 12-core, 16-core, and 24-core desktop CPUs, six cores are still considered the baseline for a decent gaming PC. Just look at how many entry-level Ryzen CPUs still ship with six cores today. Of course, that doesn't mean the good old i7-8700K can hold its own against these newer chips because CPU architectures have come a long way over the past nine years. But if these CPUs can still handle some modern games at reasonable frame rates when paired with the right GPU, I doubt most people would find them slow for everyday use.

Windows 11 officially supports these CPUs

That means no workarounds to get Windows 11 running

Intel's 8th-gen CPUs are among the oldest to support Windows 11 officially. What's funny is that even the first-gen Ryzen and mainstream 7th-gen Intel CPUs, which also launched in 2017, aren't officially supported. Sure, you can still get Windows 11 running by bypassing its hardware requirements, but I wouldn't want to deal with that if I were putting together a PC for everyday use. The fact that you can get a CPU that made the cut for less than $70 is a pretty big deal, especially now that Windows 10 has reached end of support.

Now, you could argue the CPU isn't the only thing Microsoft checks when you install Windows 11, since your PC also needs to support TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot. But that shouldn't be a problem with Z370 and Z390 motherboards. Intel's Platform Trust Technology (PTT) takes care of the TPM requirement, although you may have to enable it in the BIOS along with Secure Boot. So if you don't want to bother with bypassing the CPU requirement, I think Intel's 8th-gen CPUs are as old as I'd be willing to go for a used build.

Buying into a dead platform isn't a great idea

But at these prices, does that even matter?

Yes, there's a catch to buying a CPU from nine years ago. You're spending money on a platform that peaked forever ago. Sure, you could upgrade to a used 9900K later if you're not happy with the performance or really need those two extra cores, but that's about as far as you can go. And let's not forget you're stuck with DDR4 and PCIe 3.0, so there's no getting around the fact that you'll have to replace your motherboard if you ever want newer features down the line.

But then again, you're barely spending over $100 on the CPU and motherboard. And that's assuming you're going for the i7-8700K. You could even get an i5-8600K for under $40 and save even more money if you like. Of course, RAM is going to be expensive if you don't already have some DDR4 lying around, but even at these outrageous prices, you can still get a 16GB kit for a little over $100. So if you really need a PC right now but don't want to burn a hole in your wallet trying to build one with newer parts, I think Intel's Coffee Lake makes for a great stopgap option.

Intel's 8th-gen CPUs help you get by, and that's what matters

In an ideal world, we wouldn't even be talking about buying a used nine-year-old CPU in 2026. But this isn't an ideal world, and with component prices showing no signs of coming down anytime soon, I think we need to reconsider parts most people would've written off years ago to find value. I wouldn't really call the i7-8700K a gaming CPU anymore, but it can still handle newer titles, provided you're realistic about the kind of performance to expect. And if you just want a general-purpose PC, I think even an i5-8600 or i5-8400 should be more than enough for the next few years. It all comes down to whether these CPUs are still good enough, and for the price, it's hard to say they aren't.

But if these CPUs can still handle some modern games at reasonable frame rates when paired with the right GPU, I doubt most people would find them slow for everyday use.

Windows 11 officially supports these CPUs

That means no workarounds to get Windows 11 running

Intel's 8th-gen CPUs are among the oldest to support Windows 11 officially. What's funny is that even the first-gen Ryzen and mainstream 7th-gen Intel CPUs, which also launched in 2017, aren't officially supported. Sure, you can still get Windows 11 running by bypassing its hardware requirements, but I wouldn't want to deal with that if I were putting together a PC for everyday use. The fact that you can get a CPU that made the cut for less than $70 is a pretty big deal, especially now that Windows 10 has reached end of support.

Now, you could argue the CPU isn't the only thing Microsoft checks when you install Windows 11, since your PC also needs to support TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot. But that shouldn't be a problem with Z370 and Z390 motherboards. Intel's Platform Trust Technology (PTT) takes care of the TPM requirement, although you may have to enable it in the BIOS along with Secure Boot. So if you don't want to bother with bypassing the CPU requirement, I think Intel's 8th-gen CPUs are as old as I'd be willing to go for a used build.

Buying into a dead platform isn't a great idea

But at these prices, does that even matter?

Yes, there's a catch to buying a CPU from nine years ago. You're spending money on a platform that peaked forever ago. Sure, you could upgrade to a used 9900K later if you're not happy with the performance or really need those two extra cores, but that's about as far as you can go. And let's not forget you're stuck with DDR4 and PCIe 3.0, so there's no getting around the fact that you'll have to replace your motherboard if you ever want newer features down the line.

But then again, you're barely spending over $100 on the CPU and motherboard. And that's assuming you're going for the i7-8700K. You could even get an i5-8600K for under $40 and save even more money if you like. Of course, RAM is going to be expensive if you don't already have some DDR4 lying around, but even at these outrageous prices, you can still get a 16GB kit for a little over $100. So if you really need a PC right now but don't want to burn a hole in your wallet trying to build one with newer parts, I think Intel's Coffee Lake makes for a great stopgap option.

Intel's 8th-gen CPUs help you get by, and that's what matters

In an ideal world, we wouldn't even be talking about buying a used nine-year-old CPU in 2026. But this isn't an ideal world, and with component prices showing no signs of coming down anytime soon, I think we need to reconsider parts most people would've written off years ago to find value. I wouldn't really call the i7-8700K a gaming CPU anymore, but it can still handle newer titles, provided you're realistic about the kind of performance to expect. And if you just want a general-purpose PC, I think even an i5-8600 or i5-8400 should be more than enough for the next few years. It all comes down to whether these CPUs are still good enough, and for the price, it's hard to say they aren't.

Pairing your watch via Wi-Fi ADB

Enter only the IP address, not the port

Tap on the modded Samsung Health Monitor APK to install it. You should now see a permissions pop-up to install apps from unknown sources. Follow the prompts to head over to the device settings and allow app installations from the file manager.

You should instantly see another pop-up with an Install button. Tap on it to install the app, and then tap on Done on the following pop-up to complete the installation.

Installing the app on the watch

Installing the modded Samsung Health Monitor app on the Galaxy Watch 4 requires ADB. If you're not familiar with installing ADB on your PC, download Dante63's Minimal ADB Fastboot tool and extract it to your desktop.

Double-click the cmd-here executable to open a command prompt window. Enable ADB debugging and Debug over Wi-Fi on your watch. Head to Settings > About watch > Software version, and tap Software version repeatedly until Developer mode unlocks. Return to Developer options, toggle on both debugging options, then tap your active Wi-Fi network to note the IP address.

5. On the following page, select the Software option and then tap on the Software version on the following page a few times to enable the Developer mode.

6. Jump back to the device settings and select Developer options. Then, tap on the toggles next to the ADB debugging and Debug over Wi-Fi settings to enable them.

7. Once connected to Wi-Fi, tap on the active connection and note down the IP address mentioned on the following page.

Back on your PC, type adb pair : and enter the pairing code displayed on your watch. This mandatory step establishes a secure handshake for modern WearOS versions. Once paired, you can use adb connect (IP only, no port) to establish the connection.

9. You should instantly see a prompt on your watch asking you if you'd like to allow debugging. Select OK if you just want to allow debugging one time, or Always allow from this computer if you don't want to repeat the process again.

Type the following ADB command, and hit Enter to install the modded Samsung Health Monitor app on the watch. For this command to work as intended, you need to have the renamed Watch.SHM.MOD.apk in the same directory as the cmd-here executable, i.e., the folder in which you installed ADB. Also, replace the X in the command mentioned below with the current version number of the APK.

adb -s "IP address" install Watch.SHM.MOD.X.X.X.XXX.dante63.apk

Once the app is installed successfully, you should see "Success" in the command prompt window. Now, disconnect from ADB using the following command.

adb disconnect

You should now be able to see the modded Samsung Health Monitor app in your watch's app drawer. When you open the modded app on your phone, your Galaxy Watch 4 should connect automatically, and you should be able to see the Blood Pressure and ECG tabs. You can follow the instructions provided in the app to set these features up. Once that's done, add the ECG and blood pressure tiles to your watch, and you're good to go.

Before you start using these features, make sure to disable ADB debugging on your Galaxy Watch 4, or it will drain your battery overnight. To do so, head back to the Developer options and tap the toggle next to the ADB debugging option.

Will this method work on other Galaxy Watch models?

This workaround uses a modded Samsung Health Monitor app, and that means it's not guaranteed to work on your specific device. The mod is continually in development and receives patches and updates from the community. While it may work on other Galaxy Watch models, your results may vary.

It's also worth mentioning that since this method uses a modded Samsung Health Monitor app, you might encounter some expected issues. In addition, you won't be able to sync blood pressure data between your watch and the Samsung Health app on your phone. However, we have a simple workaround to enable BP sync on the Galaxy Watch 4 as well.

Galaxy Watch 5 and 6 limitations

If you're rocking a Galaxy Watch 5 or 6, the standard SHM MOD method often fails on the Classic variants. You'll likely need to use specific GitHub companion tools or hunt down a custom MOD version built for Wear OS 3.1+. Furthermore, blood pressure on the Watch 5+ requires initial calibration with a traditional cuff-based monitor before the watch can track trends accurately.

Galaxy Watch 7, 8, and 9 compatibility

Newer hardware introduces the Heart Health Score and Advanced Sleep Coaching, which may have different compatibility nuances than the Watch 4. On newer watches, you must slightly long-press the power button to initiate the ECG rather than just tapping it. You can view, download, and share ECG results as PDFs directly from the Samsung Health Monitor app for your healthcare provider.

Alternative methods for stubborn watches

  • Official APK route: Users unwilling to use ADB can download the official Samsung Health Monitor APK from a trusted repository, enable "Install from Unknown Sources," and manually install it. Clear the app's cache if it crashes, and check your region settings for grayed-out features.
  • Clear Data workaround: For rooted or non-rooted users hitting snags, try clearing data for Google Play Services, Google Play Store, and Huawei Wi-Fi services (if applicable), then restart your device.

Liability and troubleshooting

Modding your watch involves flashing custom software. We are not responsible for bricked devices, warranty voids, or lost data. If you encounter an "error: too many devices" message during the ADB process, run adb kill-server in your command prompt and try again.

item.title: The best speech recognition you can run at home is absolutely tiny, and it runs on a ten-year-old laptop
item.itunes:title: The best speech recognition you can run at home is absolutely tiny, and it runs on a ten-year-old laptop
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
AI-based transcription is one of the most popular use cases of LLMs, but most tools tend to rely on offering a subscription and cloud-based transcriptions. I'm talking about tools like Whisper. Now, I've used Whisper enough for turning long interviews, voice memos and recordings into text, and it works well.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

However, in 2026, transcribing speech to text shouldn't need a subscription. I wanted something that runs locally and doesn't really need powerful hardware to boot. So, I installed Parakeet, a speech recognition model that can run on almost anything from a Raspberry Pi to a decade-old computer. I tested out both the Docker-based model and a bespoke app that gives you a pretty GUI to interact with on a Mac. Here's how it went.

You don't need powerful hardware to run Parakeet

A lightweight alternative to cloud-based transcription

I've spent years with self-hosting software. Enough to know that there's invariably tweaking needed to extract the most out of these tools. Parakeet gets the fundamentals right by keeping the model small, with borderline zero config requirements and minimal hardware requirements, making transcription possible without a dedicated graphics card. That last one might come as a surprise given that the model was developed by Nvidia. But, I digress.

So, what is Parakeet? This is an automatic speech recognition model that turns spoken audio from recordings, voice notes and even straight from the mic into text. The version I tested out was the Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 model. That's a 600 million parameter model. Small enough to not bog down a MacBook Air, but capable enough to get the job done.

As far as specs go, the quantized model takes up around 700MB of space and consumes around 2GB of RAM. That's not insignificant, but also nowhere close to what larger models need in terms of system resources.

To get started, I pulled up Parakeet in Docker. The local server is easy to deploy, and you can either use the API or point it to a file on your computer and ask it to transcribe the file. It works perfectly fine, but there's a trade-off. While this is great if you are trying to integrate the API into a broader service or tool, it isn't quite as convenient for everyday use.

I wanted a WisprFlow-like experience on my computer. That's where MacParakeet steps in.

MacParakeet makes local transcription easy on a Mac

My preferred tool for hands-free dictation

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

MacParakeet takes the same idea and model and packages it in a Mac-friendly desktop app. To start with, it comes with a proper onboarding workflow that guides you through system permissions and steps needed to ensure that the Parakeet model can be deployed everywhere. It also takes over the function key to perform the audio input workflows.

With that in mind, I set up the appropriate shortcuts, including one for hands-free mode so I wouldn't have to keep holding the function key while speaking to my computer. In fact, I dictated the entirety of this write-up in MacParakeet to see how well it worked. And let's just say the results have been interesting.

I've previously tried Nematron, which is a pretty good local transcription model as well, but I was blown away by the quality of results from Parakeet. Both in terms of speech and accuracy, Parakeet has been on point even with an accent. Not just that, the performance impact on my machine has been minimal at best. I've been using Parakeet via MacParakeet to jot down outlines for articles while walking on my treadmill, replying to emails, and working with personal notes.

For meeting recordings, I can just drop the audio files straight into Parakeet and let it transcribe the text. An added benefit of using a front end like MacParakeet has been that it lets me transcribe web-based audio using the same local Parakeet model that has performed well for me. So, you can drop in YouTube links, Instagram links and more, and the app will pull down the audio and transcribe it for you. I often use this function when I'm watching an interesting research-based video. I can pull down a transcript, save it for later reading, or even use it with a local LLM to distill key insights.

Using a front end like MacParakeet also exposes other use cases like meeting recording. The app can capture system audio and microphone input, allowing me to build my own local Otter alternative. It also supports speaker identification, making it a viable alternative to commercial solutions. Once done, these transcript files can be exported in Markdown for archival purposes.

It goes without saying that all of this runs on-device, ensuring all data, including voice recordings and transcriptions, remains fully private.

Parakeet is proof that high-quality local transcription doesn't need high-end hardware

This isn't my first foray into local AI-based, offline voice transcription, but Parakeet has been one of the best implementations I've tried out so far. It is light on resources while still delivering the accuracy that is so important for a tool like this to become a part of your workflow.

Combined with the MacParakeet front end, it gives me the entire gamut of transcription services, and the best part is that I don't need to send any of these recordings to a cloud service. Everything runs locally, on par with commercial services, making Parakeet perhaps the best on-device speech recognition model I've used.

Parakeet

Parakeet is an open-source speech recognition model developed by Nvidia that converts speech to text locally.

item.title: This Jellyfin plugin just got the overhaul I've been waiting years for, and now it's even more useful
item.itunes:title: This Jellyfin plugin just got the overhaul I've been waiting years for, and now it's even more useful
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Jellyfin is a great open-source self-hosted media server that lets you do a lot with your media. It has a huge community of enthusiasts and developers who keep adding great tools and features. A new project seems to come up daily, from new clients on every modern streaming platform to plugins that make customization and management easier.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

KefinTweaks is a front-end plugin for the server that provides customization and functionality in one place. You can add different skins and themes through compatible clients on different devices. It has a lot going on, but is straightforward to configure and use for a better Jellyfin experience.

Installing the plugin is straightforward

But some prerequisites are required

Before installing the KefinTweaks plugin, you'll need a couple of plugins. You might already have them installed on your Jellyfin server, especially if you've installed other plugins like VideoOSD Tweaks & Candy. You will need the JavaScript Installer and File Transformations plugins installed and active before starting.

Once those are installed, input the JavaScript code listed on the plugin's GitHub page in the Installer plugin and save it. Then, restart your server. Once the server is back up, the KefinTweaks plugin should appear at the bottom under the Front End Plugins section. When it appears, enable the correct build to start using it.

I didn't see it right away, and this has been common for several other users. I verified I had the JavaScript code entered correctly, completely stopped my server, and started it back up. I went back to the Plugins page, hit Ctrl+F5 to hard-refresh the page, and it showed up. Then I selected it and chose the latest version, which works with my Jellyfin 12.1 server. I was able to turn on many cards, skins, and other features.

I gave Jellyfin a Kodi makeover, and my media library felt brand-new

My media center has never looked better

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Customizing the Jellyfin experience

There are a lot of possibilities with this front-end plugin

This isn't a plugin that just slaps new skins on Jellyfin, although that's part of it; it also offers functional tweaks that make viewing and managing media more enjoyable. The skins are easy to use; I select one and then customize it further. I like the watchlists to track content I plan to view, and the series progress feature for a visual representation of where I'm at in a show, so I don't lose my spot. I also use it to select a show I'll have time to finish.

KefinTweaks is a Swiss Army Knife-style plugin that also lets me add home-screen features like infinite-scroll discovery, which is nice for large libraries. I can also add new sections like seasonal content, playlists, collections, and more. I've found playlists and collections helpful for managing shows, shorter videos, and my ripped CD collection.

I also appreciate other cool features, like being able to remove content from the Continue Watching section by closing the item. I've never been a fan of watching something for two minutes and having it show up in that row. I can also hide section titles that get in my way. It also lets me search for subtitles from providers directly from the interface.

Putting "tweaks" in the name is appropriate here since it has a ton of them. I've been customizing my Jellyfin experience with tons of different settings and have barely scratched the surface. What works and looks good on my computer might not be ideal for my phone, and vice versa.

Luckily, there are so many combination possibilities that I've had a great time getting everything just right for clients running on my devices. I can change the settings for each phone or computer. I'm not stuck with the same theme or feature set everywhere. It keeps things interesting.

4 free Jellyfin tools that make my media server feel like a premium streaming service

I've caught the automation bug, I'm afraid

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Multiple platform support

Tweak Jellyfin at home or on the go

The plugin works with compatible clients that use Jellyfin Web to access the server. For instance, I can access it from a web browser, Jellyfin Media Player on a computer, or the official Android and iOS clients on my phones. But it doesn't work natively on Android TV yet. Development is also underway for other Smart TV platforms like LG webOS and Samsung Tizen.

The plugin is installed on my server and available to compatible clients across platforms. However, the KefinTweaks plugin isn't a skin or feature set that every client can see and use. But certain apps like Streamyfin and Pelagica can share the watchlist, as it is an integrated feature in both. Popular third-party clients like Moonfin and Findroid retain their own interface, so the plugin isn't compatible.

This open-source media player finally unified my Jellyfin library and YouTube into one interface

Fathom combines Jellyfin, YouTube and media requests into a single player — and it's a game changer for cord-cutters

1
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Jellyfin your way with the KefinTweaks plugin

The plugin offers so much that you'll find weeks of enjoyment just changing options and tweaking the tweaks. What's more, I can apply a skin, then add or remove CSS modules to configure it further. Plus, I can adjust every KefinTweaks setting that I implement.

With so much going on, it adds even more depth to what I can do to make my home screen functional with my media. Plus, with the right skin combination, it looks good — all while I have fun making changes.

item.title: You can ignore the hype around Wi-Fi 8 and even Wi-Fi 7 if you're already on Wi-Fi 6
item.itunes:title: You can ignore the hype around Wi-Fi 8 and even Wi-Fi 7 if you're already on Wi-Fi 6
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
There's a lot of talk about upgrading to a Wi-Fi 7 router to benefit from all the latest features it promises. Wi-Fi 7 routers have been around for a few years, but they still hold only a 7.2% share of Wi-Fi router generations (as of Q1 2026). So, it's only just picking up, even as the Wi-Fi 8 hype train is gathering steam. We already have Wi-Fi 8 routers from TP-Link and Asus on the market, and Wi-Fi 8 mesh systems are slated to launch in Q1 2027.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Amid all this FOMO about Wi-Fi 7 hardware and the improvements promised by Wi-Fi 8, I feel most people are getting carried away. The typical Wi-Fi user isn't using a fast enough internet plan to justify spending on a Wi-Fi 7 router. And as far as reliability and range are concerned, Wi-Fi 6 routers are already pretty capable. Neither internet affordability nor client support is spurring people to upgrade their routers, even in late 2026.

Wi-Fi 8 will focus on stability instead of speed, but I don't even care about Wi-Fi 7 yet

The core of Wi-Fi is broken and needs a rethink.

9
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Wi-Fi 8 is coming to attack fundamental Wi-Fi problems

But don't hold your breath yet

Wi-Fi 8 is poised to focus on "Ultra High Reliability (UHR)," taking a step away from yet another bandwidth boost. It will feature the same 46 Gbps maximum theoretical throughput. There are no new bands or increased channel width, and the peak modulation (4096-QAM) remains the same, too. What will change is the coordination between access points, spectrum usage efficiency, signal strength at the fringes of coverage, and packet delivery.

UHR means bringing new features like Multi-Access Point Coordination (MAPC), Distributed Resource Units (DRUs), Dynamic Sub-Band Operation (DSO), Non-Primary Channel Access (NPCA), and Unequal Modulation (UEQM). Those are too many new acronyms to wrap your head around, but the primary point is that they'll all work in tandem to improve the communication between your Wi-Fi and your neighbors'.

In a nutshell, multiple access points (not just those part of your own network) will work together to drastically reduce interference and improve signal strength where it's needed the most. Wi-Fi 8 will also allow slicing larger channels into smaller sub-channels to improve spectrum utilization, allow devices to transmit on a secondary channel if the primary one is busy, and transmit at its own maximum allowed rate instead of dragging the entire network down.

Reports indicate that the Wi-Fi 8 specification will be finalized by May 2028 — at least, that's the plan, according to IEEE. What this means, practically, is that early networking gear with draft Wi-Fi 8 specs will have been on the market for quite some time before Wi-Fi 8 client devices are truly available to the masses. The final Wi-Fi 8 specs may change a lot from the current draft, so I don't recommend buying early Wi-Fi 8 routers until Q3 2028, at least.

Wi-Fi 8 is finally fixing the real issues with Wi-Fi, and it's why I'm skipping Wi-Fi 7 entirely

Skipping Wi-Fi 7 means waiting for the real upgrade

By  Tanveer Singh

Wi-Fi 7 isn't that new, but it still hasn't delivered on its promises

It feels like Wi-Fi 7 is still rolling out

The promise of Wi-Fi 7 was Extremely High Throughput (EHT), enabled by wider bands, higher modulation, and Multi-Link Operation (MLO). After Wi-Fi 6E focused on efficiency, Wi-Fi 7 brought the conversation back to peak throughput. The problem, though, is that almost no one is equipped to enjoy that peak throughput. Even today, the availability and affordability of ISP plans determine the Wi-Fi speeds in most parts of the world, not the capabilities of the router.

Most Wi-Fi 7 features are still not really usable by most people around the world. Take MLO, for instance. Device support for true MLO, i.e., Simultaneous Transmit and Receive (STR), is reserved for high-end access points. STR needs multiple physical radios to send and receive data across two or more bands simultaneously, which is non-existent on battery-powered devices like phones and laptops. Plus, many devices support MLO only on the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.

Then, there's the much-touted 320 MHz channel width that exists only on the 6 GHz band, which isn't available everywhere due to licensing regulations. Furthermore, many "Wi-Fi 7" client devices only support up to 160 MHz channels. Both the 6GHz band and the 320 MHz channels struggle with range and obstacles, making them usable only when you're in the vicinity of the router.

When you remove all the fancy features of Wi-Fi 7, what remains is a theoretical boost to the maximum throughput. And with most people in the world limited to just over 100 Mbps median broadband speed (300 Mbps in the US), Wi-Fi 7 isn't really the upgrade everyone says it is.

Wi-Fi 7 routers promised the future but delivered a compatibility nightmare

It's not all rosy on the early-adopter front

9
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Wi-Fi 6 is more than enough for most people

Even for Gigabit internet

Wi-Fi is still in the future, and Wi-Fi 7 is, well, mostly useless and overpriced for the vast majority of the global user base. Even if you're still using a Wi-Fi 6 router like myself, you're perfectly placed to enjoy almost all the benefits of modern Wi-Fi. Your router is capable of a little over 1 Gbps in wireless speeds, so your internet plan is most likely within the bounds of your Wi-Fi 6 backbone.

In terms of range, a typical Wi-Fi 6 router can cover up to 2,500 sq. ft. of space without leaving dead zones. Thanks to OFDMA and MU-MIMO, your Wi-Fi 6 router can communicate with multiple devices at the same time, maintaining concurrent data streams. Of course, the real performance depends on your internet plan, but as long as you have 300–500 Mbps of bandwidth, you're not missing out on anything.

Wi-Fi 6E is only necessary when your devices can make use of the 6 GHz band, and you have the internet speed to justify the upgrade.
